meta.title: Mandarin Chinese — Pinyin and tones
meta.subtitle: 68 sounds, tones and tone changes — start here, beside Level 1
meta.desc: How pinyin is read, before or beside the first word: 68 notes, one card each — the five tone marks, where the mark is written, the three tone changes every beginner meets (two third tones together, 不, 一), the 24 initials (the 21 consonants and y, w, yu) and the 35 finals. The front shows the letters; the back gives the sound in the International Phonetic Alphabet, how it is made or what it resembles, how it is written with no consonant before it, and up to three words from the Level 1 to 3 decks with a speaker beside each, the syllable in question picked out. Say it, then press the speaker and compare: the letters j, q, x, z, c, zh, ch, sh, r and ü do not have their English values, and 165 of Level 1's 300 words contain one of them. THE ORDER is tones, tone changes, initials (b p m f, d t n l, g k h, j q x, zh ch sh r, z c s), finals. At the default of ten new cards a day the deck takes 7 days; it is meant to be studied beside Level 1, not finished first. — WHAT IS NOT HERE: no description is written for this deck. Each is quoted from the article named below, with a cut marked […]; where the article has no English comparison the card has none. The speaker is your device's Mandarin voice reading the example word, so a device without one is silent. The final weng is left out: no word of Levels 1 to 3 has it. — Sounds, descriptions and rules: Wikipedia, “Pinyin”, revision 1384755350 of 2026-11-09, and Wikipedia, “Standard Chinese phonology”, revision 1384691172 of 2026-11-09 (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example words, readings and meanings: the HSK 3.0 Level 1 to 3 decks on this shelf (the official HSK 3.0 vocabulary lists, and CC-CEDICT, CC BY-SA 4.0).

pinyin.name: Mandarin sounds

fields.Says: First tone is a high-level tone. It is a steady high sound, produced as if it were being sung instead of spoken.
fields.Note: Pitch is given on a five-level scale, 1 the lowest and 5 the highest.
fields.Examples:
as in
他tāhe
一yīone
三sānthree

fields.Says: Second tone is a rising tone. It is usually described as a high-rising (35), with the sound that rises from middle to high pitch (like in the English "What?!").
fields.Note: Pitch is given on a five-level scale, 1 the lowest and 5 the highest.
fields.Examples:
as in
您nínyou [polite form]
十shíten
零língzero

fields.Says: Third tone is a low tone. It is also often termed a "dipping tone". This tone is often demonstrated as having a rise in pitch after the low fall; […] When a third-tone syllable is not said in isolation, this rise is normally heard only if it appears at the end of a sentence or before a pause, and then usually only on stressed monosyllables.
fields.Note: Pitch is given on a five-level scale, 1 the lowest and 5 the highest.
fields.Examples:
as in
请qǐngto invite
我wǒI
你nǐyou

fields.Says: Fourth tone is a falling tone. It features a sharp fall from high to lower pitch (as is heard in curt commands in English, such as "Stop!").
fields.Note: Pitch is given on a five-level scale, 1 the lowest and 5 the highest.
fields.Examples:
as in
是shìto be
不bùnot
二èrtwo

fields.Says: Also called fifth tone or zeroth tone […], the neutral tone is sometimes thought of as a lack of tone. It is associated with weak syllables, which are generally somewhat shorter than tonic syllables. […] The pitch of a syllable with neutral tone is determined by the tone of the preceding syllable.
fields.Examples:
as in
的deof
吗ma[makes a yes-or-no question]
们men[plural marker, for pronouns and for nouns naming people]

fields.Says: If there is an a or an e, it will take the tone mark. In the combination ou, then the o takes the tone mark. Otherwise, the second vowel takes the tone mark.
fields.Examples:
as in
你好nǐ hǎohello
谢谢xiè xieto thank
对duìcorrect, right
六liùsix
有yǒuto have

fields.Says: When there are two consecutive third-tone syllables, the first of them is pronounced with second tone. Tone sandhi is not ordinarily reflected in pinyin spelling.
fields.Examples:
as in
你好nǐ hǎosaid ní hǎohello
可以kě yǐsaid ké yǐcan, may, to be permitted
水果shuǐ guǒsaid shuí guǒfruit

fields.Says: 不 is pronounced with second tone when followed by a fourth tone syllable. In other cases, 不 is pronounced with fourth tone.
fields.Note: The Level 1 deck writes this change: bú before a fourth tone.
fields.Examples:
as in
不bùnot
不客气bú kè qiimpolite, rude
不要bú yàodon't!

fields.Says: 一 is pronounced with second tone when followed by a fourth tone syllable. Before a first, second or third tone syllable, 一 is pronounced with fourth tone. When final, or when it comes at the end of a multi-syllable word (regardless of the first tone of the next word), 一 is pronounced with first tone.
fields.Note: The Level 1 deck writes this change: yí before a fourth tone, yì before the others.
fields.Examples:
as in
一yīone
一下yí xiàa bit
一些yì xiēsome
一点儿yì diǎnra bit

fields.Note: Y, w, and yu are equivalent to the semivowel medials i, u, and ü. They are spelled differently when there is no initial consonant in order to mark a new syllable.
